title: Three duties that aren't about comparators at all
subtitle: Harassment, victimisation and the duty to make reasonable adjustments
objectives: State the s 26 test for harassment and the s 27 test for victimisation, and explain why neither requires a comparator
Identify the two distinct triggers for the duty to make reasonable adjustments under ss 20-21 — a PCP and a physical feature
Apply all three provisions to new fact patterns and distinguish them from each other and from direct/indirect discrimination

leadingAuthorities.role: Defines harassment: unwanted conduct related to a protected characteristic that violates dignity or creates a hostile environment
Defines victimisation: subjecting someone to detriment because they did a protected act
The duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled employees, triggered by a PCP or a physical feature

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This lesson covers three provisions students routinely mix up with each other and with the discrimination tests from Lessons 9 and 10. None of the three needs a comparator — that's the thread connecting them, and it's exactly what an exam question will be probing when it drops you into a fact pattern with no obvious 'treated less favourably than whom' moment. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can define all three — the test here is telling them apart on the facts.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. This test pool is weighted heavily towards scenarios that could plausibly be harassment, victimisation, or a reasonable adjustments failure — expect to justify why one applies and not the others.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and fix the elements of each provision precisely before moving on — this lesson only gets harder if you're vague on where s 26 ends and s 27 begins.

overview.hook: A colleague makes the same joke about your accent every week for a year. You complain to HR. Three weeks later you're passed over for a project you were the obvious choice for. None of that story needs a comparator — no one has to show a colleague without your accent was treated better, or that someone else who didn't complain got the project instead. This lesson is about the parts of the Equality Act that don't run on comparison at all.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. Sections 20-21 and 26-27 Equality Act 2010 are stable, long-settled provisions; no legislative change to them is currently pending.

parts.heading: Harassment: conduct, not comparison
parts.voice: structural — establishes the test before the illustrative case
body: Section 26 Equality Act 2010 defines harassment as unwanted conduct related to a relevant protected characteristic which has the purpose or effect of violating the claimant's dignity, or creating an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment for them. Read that carefully: it's 'related to' a characteristic, not 'because of' one — a broader test than direct discrimination's causal requirement, catching conduct connected to a characteristic even where the harasser wasn't targeting the claimant's own characteristic specifically (a colleague subjected to racist jokes about a different group, who finds the environment hostile as a result, can potentially claim).

The test has both a subjective and an objective element, and both must be satisfied. Subjectively, the conduct must actually have had the purpose or effect the claimant describes — it must genuinely have violated their dignity or created that environment for them. Objectively, in deciding whether conduct had that effect, a tribunal must take into account the claimant's perception, the other circumstances of the case, and whether it is reasonable for the conduct to have that effect. A claimant who is unusually sensitive, and reacts to conduct that reasonably wouldn't have that effect on anyone, will not succeed on the objective limb even if their subjective reaction was genuine.

Notice, too, what harassment doesn't require: no less favourable treatment, no comparator, and — for most protected characteristics — no need to show the claimant personally has the characteristic in question. A single, sufficiently serious incident can be enough; it doesn't need to be a pattern, though a pattern strengthens the claim considerably.

components.text: A person (A) harasses another (B) if — (a) A engages in unwanted conduct related to a relevant protected characteristic, and (b) the conduct has the purpose or effect of — (i) violating B's dignity, or (ii) creating an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment for B.
elements: Related to a relevant protected characteristic
Purpose or effect of violating dignity, or creating a hostile/intimidating/degrading/humiliating/offensive environment
Subjective effect on B plus an objective reasonableness check on whether that effect was reasonable

components.definition: The causal link required for harassment under s 26 is deliberately looser than direct discrimination's 'because of' test — conduct can be related to a protected characteristic without being directed at the claimant's own characteristic, and without any comparator being needed at all.

interaction.prompt: Does a harassment claim under s 26 require the claimant to identify a comparator who was treated better?
options: No — harassment has no comparator requirement at all
Yes — a comparator is required in the same way as for direct discrimination
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Harassment is defined entirely by the conduct and its effect on the claimant — there's no 'treated less favourably than' step anywhere in s 26.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — this is one of the features that most sharply distinguishes harassment from direct discrimination. Section 26 never asks how someone else was treated; it asks only about the conduct and its effect on the claimant.

parts.heading: Victimisation: the retaliation provision
parts.voice: direct — works from the statutory text to the practical trap
body: Section 27 protects anyone who does a 'protected act' from being subjected to a detriment because they did it. The protected acts are listed exhaustively in s 27(2): bringing proceedings under the Act, giving evidence or information in connection with proceedings under the Act, doing any other thing for the purposes of or in connection with the Act, and making an allegation (whether or not express) that someone has contravened the Act.

This provision exists for an obvious structural reason: discrimination law only works if people are actually willing to complain about it, give evidence about it, and support colleagues who do. Without protection against retaliation, every other right in the Act would be undermined by employees' entirely rational fear of the consequences of raising a claim.

Two traps recur in application questions. First, the detriment doesn't need to follow a successful discrimination claim — a genuine but ultimately unsuccessful complaint, made in good faith, is still a protected act, and retaliating against someone for having made it is still victimisation. Second, s 27(3) excludes from protection an allegation that is itself false and made in bad faith — but a mistaken, honestly held allegation remains protected even if it turns out to be wrong.

components.text: (1) A person (A) victimises another person (B) if A subjects B to a detriment because — (a) B does a protected act, or (b) A believes B has done, or may do, a protected act. (2) Each of the following is a protected act — (a) bringing proceedings under this Act; (b) giving evidence or information in connection with proceedings under this Act; (c) doing any other thing for the purposes of or in connection with this Act; (d) making an allegation (whether or not express) that A or another person has contravened this Act.
elements: A subjects B to a detriment
Because B did (or A believes B did or may do) a protected act
Protected acts include bringing proceedings, giving evidence, or making an allegation of a contravention
A genuine but unsuccessful complaint is still protected; a false allegation made in bad faith is not

interaction.prompt: Put these events in the order needed to establish a s 27 victimisation claim.
items: B does a protected act (e.g. raises a genuine discrimination complaint)
A becomes aware of, or believes, B has done the protected act
A subjects B to a detriment
B shows the detriment was because of the protected act
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the structure: the protected act comes first, A's awareness or belief follows, then a detriment, and finally the causal link tying the detriment to the protected act.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order — a s 27 claim starts with the protected act itself, then requires A's awareness or belief of it, then a detriment, and finally the causal link between the two.

parts.heading: Reasonable adjustments: a duty triggered two different ways
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: The duty to make reasonable adjustments, in ss 20-21 Equality Act 2010, is unlike anything else in this module: it's a positive duty to act, owed only to disabled people, and it applies even where there's been no 'less favourable treatment' of anyone. Failing to make a reasonable adjustment is itself a freestanding form of discrimination.

The duty comprises three requirements, but two matter most for an LLB syllabus. The first requirement applies where a PCP puts a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage compared with non-disabled people — the employer must take reasonable steps to avoid that disadvantage. The third requirement applies where a physical feature of premises puts a disabled person at that same substantial disadvantage — again, reasonable steps must be taken to avoid it, which might mean removing the feature, altering it, or providing a reasonable means of avoiding it.

'Substantial' means more than minor or trivial — a deliberately low bar, lower than the threshold for other disadvantage tests in the Act. What's 'reasonable' is fact-specific and considers factors including the cost and practicality of the step, the employer's resources, and how effective the step would actually be at removing the disadvantage. Crucially, the duty is anticipatory and proactive in the employment context — an employer who knows, or ought reasonably to know, that an employee has a disability and may be placed at a substantial disadvantage cannot simply wait to be asked; a failure to act is itself the breach.

components.label: The two triggers for the duty (ss 20-21)
points: PCP trigger — a provision, criterion or practice puts a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage compared with non-disabled people
Physical feature trigger — a physical feature of premises puts a disabled person at that substantial disadvantage
In both cases: the employer must take such steps as it is reasonable to take to avoid the disadvantage
'Substantial' means more than minor or trivial — a low threshold
Failure to comply with the duty is, by itself, a form of unlawful discrimination — no comparator, no PCP applied to everyone, required

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that identifies the trigger for the duty to make reasonable adjustments in this scenario.
interaction.scenarioText: Tomasz, who uses a wheelchair, works on the third floor of an office building. The only route to his desk is via a staircase, with no lift installed. He asks his employer to relocate his desk to the ground floor, and the request is refused without any consideration of alternatives.
tappableSpans: asks his employer to relocate his desk
refused without any consideration of alternatives
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — the absence of a lift is a physical feature of the premises putting Tomasz at a substantial disadvantage compared with non-wheelchair-using colleagues. That's the s 20-21 trigger; the refusal afterwards is the breach, not the trigger itself.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the feature of the workplace itself causing the disadvantage, not the request or the refusal. The absence of a lift is the physical feature that triggers the duty under s 20-21.

parts.heading: Telling the three apart on the facts
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the puzzle before resolving it
body: Here's the skill this lesson is really testing: given a messy fact pattern, which of harassment, victimisation, and reasonable adjustments — if any — actually applies? The three provisions can look similar on the surface (none needs a comparator, all can arise from workplace conduct) but they answer completely different questions.

Ask three questions in order. Is the complaint about conduct that made the workplace hostile or degrading, connected to a protected characteristic? That's harassment territory. Is it about someone being punished, sidelined or disadvantaged specifically because they complained, gave evidence, or alleged a contravention of the Act? That's victimisation. Is it about a disabled employee being left at a substantial disadvantage by a rule or a physical feature that the employer failed to adjust? That's the reasonable adjustments duty.

The three can overlap on the same facts — a disabled employee who raises a reasonable adjustments complaint, is then subjected to hostile comments about 'making a fuss,' and is later overlooked for a promotion, potentially has claims for a failure to adjust, harassment, and victimisation all arising from one connected sequence of events. Spotting all three, and explaining what each adds, is exactly what a strong exam answer does that a weak one doesn't.

components.title: Which provision applies?
components.description: A decision path for classifying a workplace complaint among harassment, victimisation and the reasonable adjustments duty.

nodes.label: Is the complaint about conduct creating a hostile/degrading/offensive environment, connected to a protected characteristic?
No → is it about a detriment following a complaint, evidence, or allegation under the Act?
No → is it about a disabled employee disadvantaged by a PCP or physical feature, with no adjustment made?
Yes → consider the ss 20-21 duty to make reasonable adjustments
No → consider direct (s 13) or indirect (s 19) discrimination instead

components.textAlternative: First ask whether the complaint is about conduct creating a hostile, degrading or offensive environment connected to a protected characteristic — if so, consider harassment under s 26. If not, ask whether it's about a detriment following a complaint, evidence, or allegation under the Act — if so, consider victimisation under s 27. If not, ask whether it's about a disabled employee disadvantaged by a PCP or physical feature with no adjustment made — if so, consider the reasonable adjustments duty under ss 20-21. If none of these fit, consider direct or indirect discrimination instead.

interaction.prompt: Which scenario is best classified as victimisation rather than harassment?
interaction.scenarioA: A manager repeatedly makes derogatory comments about a colleague's religion in team meetings, making the employee dread coming to work.
interaction.scenarioB: An employee who gave a witness statement supporting a colleague's discrimination claim is subsequently excluded from team meetings and denied a bonus she was previously told she'd receive.
interaction.explanation: B is victimisation: the detriment (exclusion, denied bonus) follows directly from a protected act (giving evidence in connection with proceedings under the Act). A is harassment: conduct related to a protected characteristic creating a hostile environment, with no protected act or retaliation in sight.

parts.heading: Reasonable adjustments in practice: what counts as reasonable
parts.voice: case-narrative — walks through a worked scenario before generalising
body: Consider Halima, a paralegal with a chronic fatigue condition that qualifies as a disability under the Act. Her firm operates a strict policy requiring all staff to be in the office from 9am, with no exceptions. Halima's condition means mornings are consistently harder for her, and she asks to start at 10.30am, making up the time later in the day. Is the employer obliged to agree?

Work through the duty in order. The PCP is the fixed 9am start. It puts Halima, because of her disability, at a substantial disadvantage compared with non-disabled colleagues who can comply without difficulty — this is not a minor or trivial difficulty; it's a condition that makes the fixed time genuinely harder to meet. That triggers the duty. The remaining question is what step is reasonable: cost, practicality and effectiveness all matter. If Halima's role doesn't require her to be present at 9am for any operational reason — no client calls, no team handovers depending on it — a flexible start time is likely to be both effective and low-cost, and a tribunal would likely find refusing it unreasonable.

Now vary the facts: suppose Halima's role is answering an emergency out-of-hours legal helpline that opens at 9am sharp, and no other staff member is qualified to cover that specific slot. The disadvantage and the trigger are unchanged — but the reasonableness of the particular adjustment requested may now be different, because the operational cost of granting exactly that adjustment is much higher. The employer would still need to consider whether some other adjustment — cover arrangements, a different task allocation — could achieve the same protective effect at lower cost, rather than simply refusing outright.

components.caseName: Illustrative scenario: Halima, chronic fatigue and a fixed start time
components.citation: Worked example — not a reported case
components.factsShort: A disabled employee's chronic fatigue makes a rigid 9am start substantially harder to meet than for non-disabled colleagues.
components.ratioShort: The duty asks first whether a PCP creates a substantial disadvantage, then separately whether the specific adjustment requested is a reasonable step given cost, practicality and effectiveness.

expanded.facts: A firm's blanket 9am start policy disadvantages an employee whose disability makes mornings harder, and she requests a later, flexible start with hours made up later in the day.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Illustrative only: the analysis proceeds by first confirming the PCP (the fixed start time), then the substantial disadvantage (mornings being harder because of the disability), then asking what step would be reasonable given the operational context.
expanded.significance: This worked example shows the duty operates in two analytically separate stages — establishing the trigger, then assessing reasonableness — and that the same trigger can lead to different conclusions on reasonableness depending on the operational facts, which is exactly the kind of variation exam scenarios exploit.

interaction.prompt: An accountancy firm requires all staff to complete an in-person induction day with no remote alternative offered. Beatriz, who has severe social anxiety that qualifies as a disability, finds the format overwhelming and asks to complete an equivalent induction via recorded materials and a one-to-one video call instead. The firm refuses, citing 'consistency' with no further explanation. Analyse whether the firm has breached the ss 20-21 duty.
factsToOrder: The firm requires an in-person induction day for all staff, with no remote alternative
Beatriz has social anxiety qualifying as a disability
The format is substantially harder for her because of her disability
She proposes an alternative (recorded materials plus a video call)

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the firm's refusal to allow an alternative induction format breaches the ss 20-21 duty to make reasonable adjustments.
modelAnswer.rule: Sections 20-21 require an employer to take reasonable steps to avoid a substantial disadvantage caused to a disabled person by a PCP, where 'substantial' means more than minor or trivial and reasonableness turns on factors including cost, practicality and effectiveness of the proposed step.
modelAnswer.application: The mandatory in-person induction is a PCP. It causes Beatriz a substantial disadvantage compared with non-disabled colleagues, given her social anxiety makes the format overwhelming rather than merely inconvenient. This triggers the duty. Beatriz has identified a specific, apparently low-cost and effective alternative (recorded materials plus a one-to-one call) that would achieve the same induction purpose. The firm's stated reason — 'consistency' alone, with no further detail about cost, practicality or actual operational need — does not engage with reasonableness at all; it looks like the kind of bare assertion that fails to justify refusing an otherwise workable adjustment.
modelAnswer.conclusion: On these facts, the firm is likely in breach of the ss 20-21 duty: the trigger is clearly established and the refusal, on the reasoning given, does not show the proposed adjustment was actually unreasonable.

testPool.prompt: Name the statutory provision defining harassment and its core elements in one sentence.
acceptableAnswers: s 26 Equality Act 2010 — unwanted conduct related to a protected characteristic that violates dignity or creates a hostile environment
section 26, unwanted conduct related to a characteristic with the purpose or effect of violating dignity or creating a hostile environment
testPool.modelAnswer: Section 26 Equality Act 2010: unwanted conduct related to a relevant protected characteristic which has the purpose or effect of violating the claimant's dignity or creating an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment for them.

testPool.prompt: Under s 26, must conduct be 'because of' a protected characteristic, as with direct discrimination, or is a looser test used?
options: A looser test — the conduct need only be 'related to' the characteristic
The same 'because of' test as direct discrimination

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a protected act under s 27(2)?
options: Bringing proceedings under the Equality Act 2010
Giving evidence in connection with proceedings under the Act
Making a false allegation known by the claimant to be untrue
Making an allegation, express or otherwise, that someone has contravened the Act
testPool.trapExplanation: Section 27(3) removes protection from an allegation that is false and made in bad faith. A genuine but mistaken allegation remains protected; the exclusion is narrow and targets dishonesty, not being wrong.

testPool.prompt: Under ss 20-21, what are the two triggers for the duty to make reasonable adjustments covered in this lesson?
options: A provision, criterion or practice, or a physical feature of premises
Direct discrimination and indirect discrimination
A written complaint and a tribunal claim

testPool.prompt: Order the analytical steps for assessing a reasonable adjustments claim.
items: Identify the PCP or physical feature in question
Confirm it puts a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage compared with non-disabled people
Identify what step(s) might avoid that disadvantage
Assess whether taking that step was reasonable, given cost, practicality and effectiveness

testPool.prompt: In the extract below, highlight the phrase that shows harassment does not require a comparator.
testPool.passage: A person harasses another if they engage in unwanted conduct related to a relevant protected characteristic, and the conduct has the purpose or effect of violating that person's dignity or creating a hostile environment for them. The test asks only about the conduct and its effect on the claimant, not about how anyone else was treated.
testPool.ratioSentence: The test asks only about the conduct and its effect on the claimant, not about how anyone else was treated.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that identifies the protected act in this scenario.
testPool.scenarioText: Ravi tells HR he believes a colleague was passed over for promotion because of her pregnancy. Two weeks later, Ravi's manager removes him from a high-profile client account with no explanation.
tappableSpans: passed over for promotion because of her pregnancy
removes him from a high-profile client account
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right — raising the allegation with HR is the protected act under s 27(2)(d); everything after it (the timing and the removal from the account) goes to detriment and causation, not to identifying the protected act itself.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the moment Ravi makes an allegation connected to the Act — that's the protected act. The removal from the account afterwards is the detriment, not the protected act.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is best analysed as a failure to make reasonable adjustments rather than harassment?
testPool.scenarioA: A deaf employee is not provided with a British Sign Language interpreter for compulsory team briefings, despite repeated requests, and consistently misses information given to hearing colleagues.
testPool.scenarioB: A colleague repeatedly mimics a deaf employee's speech patterns in front of the team, causing him distress.
testPool.explanation: A concerns a PCP (compulsory briefings with no interpreter) causing a substantial disadvantage with no step taken to remove it — a reasonable adjustments issue. B is conduct related to the characteristic creating a hostile or humiliating environment — that's harassment, not a failure to adjust.

testPool.prompt: An employee raises a grievance alleging sex discrimination in good faith, but the grievance is ultimately not upheld after investigation. Her manager subsequently excludes her from a project team, telling colleagues she 'causes trouble.' Does she have a viable victimisation claim?
options: Yes — a genuine complaint made in good faith is a protected act even if it is not ultimately upheld, and exclusion following it is a detriment
No — only a successful discrimination complaint counts as a protected act
No — victimisation requires the same protected characteristic as the original complaint
testPool.explanation: The outcome of the original complaint is irrelevant to whether it was a protected act; what matters is that it was genuine and not made in bad faith. Exclusion from the project, linked to the complaint, is a textbook detriment for victimisation purposes.

testPool.prompt: An employer knows an employee has dyslexia but has never been asked to make any adjustment. The employee is disadvantaged by a PCP requiring all internal assessments to be completed in a fixed, unmodified written format, and the employer never considers whether an adjustment might be needed. Is the employer's inaction potentially a breach of ss 20-21, even without a specific request?
options: Yes — the duty is proactive; an employer who knows, or ought reasonably to know, of the disability and disadvantage cannot simply wait to be asked
No — the duty only arises once the employee makes an explicit written request for an adjustment
No — the duty only applies to physical features of premises, not to assessment formats
testPool.explanation: The reasonable adjustments duty is anticipatory in the employment context. Once the employer has the relevant knowledge, failing to consider or make an adjustment can itself be the breach — a formal request is not a precondition of the duty arising.

testPool.prompt: Must the disadvantage caused by a PCP under ss 20-21 be severe to trigger the duty?
options: No — 'substantial' means more than minor or trivial, a deliberately low threshold
Yes — only severe, life-altering disadvantage triggers the duty

testPool.prompt: Jian, a warehouse operative with a visual impairment, is repeatedly mocked by two colleagues who imitate him bumping into shelving, in front of the rest of the team. He reports this to his supervisor. A month later, his shifts are cut from full-time to part-time, and he is told this is 'just how the rota worked out.' Analyse what claims, if any, Jian may have under ss 26 and 27 Equality Act 2010.
factsToOrder: Colleagues repeatedly mock Jian's visual impairment in front of the team
Jian reports the conduct to his supervisor
A month later his shifts are cut from full-time to part-time
The employer offers only a vague, unexplained justification for the change

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Jian has a harassment claim under s 26 arising from the mocking conduct, and a separate victimisation claim under s 27 arising from the reduction in his hours.
modelAnswer.rule: Section 26 requires unwanted conduct related to a protected characteristic having the purpose or effect of violating dignity or creating a hostile/humiliating environment. Section 27 requires a detriment because the claimant did, or was believed to have done, a protected act, including making an allegation of a contravention of the Act.
modelAnswer.application: The repeated mocking of Jian's visual impairment is unwanted conduct related to a protected characteristic, and mimicking him in front of the team is capable of creating a humiliating or hostile environment — a strong s 26 claim. His report to his supervisor is itself a protected act under s 27(2)(d) (an allegation connected to the Act), even informally made. The reduction in his hours a month later is a detriment; the vague, unexplained 'rota' justification does little to rebut an inference of a causal link given the timing, which a tribunal would likely find suspicious absent a credible, evidenced business reason.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Jian has a strong harassment claim based on the mocking conduct and a viable victimisation claim based on the subsequent reduction in his hours, given the weak and unexplained justification offered for the timing.

testPool.prompt: An employee who is not disabled, but who cares for a disabled family member, is mocked by colleagues for 'always leaving early for hospital appointments.' Could this amount to harassment under s 26?
options: No — s 26 only protects employees who personally have the protected characteristic
Yes — conduct can be 'related to' a protected characteristic (disability, via the family member) without the claimant personally holding that characteristic
No — harassment can never arise from comments about a third party
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to assume harassment only protects people who personally hold the characteristic, mirroring the more restrictive comparator logic of direct discrimination. But the 'related to' language in s 26 is broader, and conduct connected to a family member's disability, creating a hostile environment for the employee themselves, can fall within it.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that a single, sufficiently serious incident can amount to harassment under s 26, without needing to be part of a repeated pattern?
sliderLabels: Not confident — a pattern is always required
Confident — a single incident can be enough
testPool.correctPosition: Confident — a single incident can be enough
testPool.explanation: Correct. Section 26 does not require repetition; a single incident, if it has the purpose or effect described in the section, is capable of amounting to harassment, though repeated conduct will often strengthen the claim on the facts.

testPool.prompt: Name the two exclusions or limits worth remembering on victimisation: what removes protection from an allegation, and what is not required for the underlying complaint to count as a protected act?
acceptableAnswers: a false allegation made in bad faith is excluded; the complaint need not succeed
bad faith false allegations are excluded under s 27(3); an unsuccessful but genuine complaint is still a protected act
testPool.modelAnswer: An allegation that is false and made in bad faith is excluded from protection under s 27(3); but a genuine complaint remains a protected act even if it is ultimately unsuccessful or not upheld.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is picking the wrong one of the three provisions — usually reaching for harassment when the facts actually describe retaliation for a complaint (victimisation), or describing hostile conduct when the real issue is an employer's failure to adjust a rule or feature. Read for what the complaint is actually about before naming the provision.
